analysis.investment_thesis: ACE Alpha Tech fails the Magic Formula on its most critical leg: with ROE of just 0.41%, return on capital is essentially zero, meaning this is a poor business regardless of price. A 12.4x P/E on near-zero earnings is not "cheap" — it's a statistical artifact of a tiny INR 156 Cr microcap with negligible profitability.
key_strengths: Modest headline P/E of 12.4 (but misleading given near-zero ROE)
Asset-light consulting model requires little fixed capital
Promoter holding of 43.9% provides some skin in the game
key_risks: ROE of 0.41% implies ROIC near zero — the business earns almost nothing on capital
INR 156 Cr microcap with negligible institutional interest (FII 0.19%, DII 0.01%)
Generic consulting/bookkeeping offering with no discernible competitive moat
red_flags: ROE of 0.41% — Magic Formula ROIC criterion catastrophically failed
Promoter holding below 50% in a small, obscure company
Earnings quality suspect — P/E of 12.4 on trivial earnings base
analysis.detailed_analysis:
The Magic Formula demands two things simultaneously: a cheap price (high earnings yield) and a good business (high return on capital). ACE Alpha Tech fails decisively on the second. A 0.41% ROE translates to essentially zero return on capital — for every rupee of equity deployed, the company generates under half a paisa of profit. No earnings yield, however attractive, can compensate for a business that doesn't compound capital. This is precisely the kind of "value trap" the Magic Formula is designed to filter out.

Furthermore, the apparent cheapness is illusory. A P/E of 12.4 on a tiny earnings base in a commoditized consulting/bookkeeping niche offers no margin of safety. There's no evidence of pricing power, scale advantage, or differentiated IP. With a sub-INR 200 Cr market cap, near-zero institutional ownership, and a generic service portfolio, this stock ranks in the bottom decile on ROIC and provides no compelling entry on earnings yield. Pass.
